name: Rosa Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Rosa, and thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Eastgate Fresh Produce, a wholesale market where restaurants and greengrocers buy their fruit and vegetables. I get in at four, walk the cold rooms, and taste or squeeze whatever came in overnight. Then I phone the growers and importers, usually the Spanish and Dutch ones, and buy for the next two days. It's a lot of standing and a lot of guessing about the weather. I'm junior here, even after seven years, since Mrs Ferraro (the buying manager) trusts her own nose more than mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the supermarkets. How is that showing up in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the smell of a good tomato at five in the morning, and I like the market people. What tires me is the hours and the knees, plus the feeling that supermarkets are slowly cutting the market out of the chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a useful assistant and no more. To friends I'd say I believe it a bit less every year, like with every new gadget. Online I'd not say much, but I'd perhaps like a post from somebody who tried it and found it was overrated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine, mostly. I use an AI tool now and then to translate emails from the Spanish growers and check prices against last year, and it helps. The worry isn't AI. It's the market itself, and my savings, which wouldn't last a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and use the translator a bit more because it's quick. I'd ask Mrs Ferraro to let me handle the citrus contracts, which would show I can do more. And I'd put 20 a week away without telling Tomasz, so it's a surprise cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels mostly steady. I get a bit tense in winter when prices jump, but there's nothing about this picture that scares me. It would be much the same as now, and now is hard but not frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save 20 a week without telling your husband. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, my husband, works nights as a cleaner at the hospital. Between us the money is enough as long as nothing breaks. If the boiler went, we'd be using the credit card, and I wouldn't like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the council sold the market land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The real danger in the plateau is the market closing or being sold off. The council has been talking about the land, and if that happened, AI wouldn't be to blame. I'd still be out, though, with few buying jobs anywhere else near here.

say: I'd say it's a **useful assistant** and no more.
I'd tell friends I believe it a bit less every year, like each **new gadget**.
think: I'd be fine, mostly, since I already use AI to **translate** and check prices.
The worry is the **market** itself and savings that wouldn't last a month.
do: **Use** the translator more, because it's quick.
**Ask** Mrs Ferraro to let me handle the citrus contracts.
**Save** 20 a week as a surprise cushion.
feel: **Steady**, with some tension in winter when prices jump.
S0.quote: The real danger in the plateau is the market closing or being sold off.
fieldNote: She is steady and keeps her focus on the **market**, not on AI.
Uses AI for translation and price checks, so the tools feel like help rather than threat.
The secret saving shows a wish to protect her husband from worry.

steps.text: Use the AI translator more for emails from Spanish growers
Carry on buying fruit and veg for the next two days each morning
Put 20 a week away as a surprise cushion for Tomasz and me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I'm happy to learn the new tools if there's a bit of time and a clear aim. To friends I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so we should get ready sensibly. Online I'd stay quiet, though I might share a fair article.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the screen part of my job gets taken first. Ordering, price checks and even choosing growers could be done by software. What's left is walking the cold rooms and judging quality, which is what I'm best at, so I might keep that bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Ferraro to make me the person who checks quality on arrival, since a machine can't squeeze a peach. I'd go on a course for the new ordering system when it comes. And I'd start putting by 60 a week and stop the Saturday coffee runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a slow change in the weather. I don't panic, but I do pay attention. I've seen the market change before, and the people who adapted were the ones who kept their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work, and what would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dilip works the cold room and he's only 29. I'd say to him that we should both learn the new system, and share what we learn. I'd rather it be two of us than one, since it's less lonely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You think quality checking is safe. What would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries me is that quality checking, which seems safe to me, might be something they'd give to a camera and a sensor. I'd want some proof from the firm before I believed it was a long-term job.

say: I'd say I'm happy to **learn** if there's some time and a clear aim.
I'd tell friends it's coming anyway, so we should **get ready** sensibly.
think: The screen part of my job goes first, but **quality checks** might be mine to keep.
What's left is walking the cold rooms, which is what I'm **best at**.
do: **Ask** Mrs Ferraro to make me the arrival quality checker.
**Go** on the course for the new ordering system.
**Put** 60 a week by and stop the Saturday coffee runs.
feel: Like a slow change in the **weather**; I pay attention, but I don't panic.
S1.quote: I'd ask Mrs Ferraro to make me the person who checks quality on arrival, since a machine can't squeeze a peach.
fieldNote: She **splits** her job into screen work and sensing work, and bets on the second.
Willing and organised, but anxious because her low-paid desk is part of the first half.
Looks for a partner in Dilip, which suits her sociable style.

steps.text: Ask Mrs Ferraro to make me the arrival quality checker
Go on the course for the new ordering system
Put 60 a week by and drop the Saturday coffee runs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a government plan right now, and an honest word from the firms. At work I'd ask Mrs Ferraro what Eastgate intends to do. With friends I'd say we shouldn't pretend it's fine, because it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd lose my job within a year or so. Even if quality checks stay with people for a while, I'd be one of the first on the screens to go. Two years isn't long enough to switch careers at 58, with no money behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Tomasz that night and agree a bare-bones budget. I'd sell my mother's old jewellery, which is worth some money, and I'd ask the bank about a hardship plan on our loan. I'd also go to the union office and ask about redundancy rights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like panic wrapped up in a coat. I'd keep a calm face for the market people, and I'd be shaking on the inside. I'd cry in the car at least once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home, and what comes next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Kasia works at the supermarket checkout, which is already half self-service. I'd say to her that we're in the same boat now. I'd hate to be asking her for help, but I think she'd offer anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk with your husband Tomasz that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What gets cut first is the car. We don't really need it, since the bus goes by the market. After that the holiday we'd planned for my sister's birthday, and then the phone upgrade. Food is the last thing to go.

say: I'd say we need a government **plan** right now and an honest word from the firms.
I'd tell Mrs Ferraro to say what Eastgate intends to do.
think: I think I'd lose my job within **a year or so**.
Two years isn't enough to switch careers at 58 with no **money behind me**.
do: **Agree** a bare-bones budget with Tomasz that night.
**Sell** my mother's old jewellery and ask the bank about a hardship plan.
**Visit** the union office about redundancy rights.
feel: Like **panic** wrapped up in a coat, calm outside and shaking inside.
S2.quote: I'd keep a calm face for the market people, and I'd be shaking on the inside.
fieldNote: She expects to lose her job and hides it from colleagues; **alarmed** despite a composed manner.
Names her cuts in order and keeps food last.
Her daughter's self-service checkout job shows the same pattern in the family.

steps.text: Agree a bare-bones budget with Tomasz the same night
Sell my mother's jewellery and ask the bank for a hardship plan
Visit the union office about redundancy rights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and we should use it. At work I'd say let's train people on the new tools together. To friends I'd say don't wait for a rescue, because nobody is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years gives me a real chance. I'd be 63, so I could move into a hands-on job like cold-room supervisor and ride the extra three years. I'd still be worried, because my savings are small and my knees aren't getting any younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first year to get certified in food safety, which is a sensible hands-on skill. I'd use the AI tools so I'm not behind. And I'd save 80 a week, hoping to have a few thousand in the bank by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like there's enough time to be sensible, so I'm not terrified. But there's a heaviness about getting everything right. It's a bit like packing for a long trip with a small suitcase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What difference does five years make compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Dilip about taking turns on the cold room, so I could learn the supervision side. I'd tell Mrs Ferraro I'm interested. She might say no, but asking costs nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said dignity matters. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots being three years behind helps people on the floor. I'd rather be in the cold room in 2032 than at a screen, even for less pay. At that point it's a bit of dignity as much as money.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning** and we should use it.
I'd tell friends **not to wait** for a rescue.
think: Five years gives me a **real chance**, maybe as a cold-room supervisor.
My savings are small and my **knees** aren't getting younger.
do: **Get** certified in food safety in the first year.
**Learn** the AI tools so I'm not behind.
**Save** 80 a week, aiming for a few thousand by 2029.
feel: **Sensible, not terrified**, though heavy about getting it all right.
S3.quote: I'd rather be in the cold room in 2032 than at a screen, even for less pay.
fieldNote: Five years lets her switch to **hands-on** work, which she explicitly links to the robot delay.
Still anxious about money and her knees.
Dignity, not only pay, drives her preference.

steps.text: Get a food safety certificate in the first year
Learn the AI ordering tools so I'm not behind
Save 80 a week, aiming for a few thousand by 2029
Ask Mrs Ferraro about cold-room supervisor work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and I'd mean it. At work I'd keep doing my job and use the tools. With friends I'd say we should stay calm and plan, and that it's fine to be curious about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68 in 2036, so I think I'd have retired by then. It's more my kids' problem than mine. My worry is that retirement on a thin pension will be tight even without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 65, save steadily and learn the tools as they come. I'd also offer to train the younger ones at Eastgate, since passing on what I know seems like a good use of the time. And I'd take a proper holiday with Tomasz while we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels pretty calm. Not carefree, since money's money, but I'm not lying awake. I'd say it's one of those worries you set at the back of the cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Kasia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kasia to leave the checkout and train for something in care or a trade. She's 34, so she's got the time. I'd even help with the course fees if I could scrape the money together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the ten years change what you'd do compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd do differently with ten years is to enjoy it. If I know I'll be out of this before it bites, I can work, save a bit, and look forward to my retirement.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time**, and I'd mean it.
I'd tell friends to stay **calm and plan**.
think: I'd be 68 in 2036, so I'd have **retired**, and it's more my kids' problem.
My worry is a **thin pension** even without AI.
do: **Work** until 65, save steadily and learn the tools as they arrive.
feel: Pretty **calm**, like a worry set at the back of the cupboard.
S4.quote: If I know I'll be out of this before it bites, I can work, save a bit, and look forward to my retirement.
fieldNote: Ten years moves AGI past her working life; her mood is **uneasy**, not calm, because money stays thin.
Sees mentoring the young as a good use of her time.
Wants to help her daughter Kasia retrain, which shows where her energy goes.

steps.text: Work until 65 and save steadily for the pension gap
Learn each new ordering tool as Eastgate brings it in
Help Kasia pay for a care or trade course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2031 one worries me most, because it's close enough to bite but too far to ignore. I'd be 63, still short of money, and the screen part of my job would go on the date. The two-year one is just too much to think about.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say don't forget the people who've been junior for a long time through no fault of their own. Some of us started late after raising kids. We're not slow, we just started late.

headlineQuote: We're not slow, we just started late.
portrait: Rosa is 58, a junior buyer at **Eastgate Fresh Produce**, a wholesale market, with a night-shift husband and two grown children.
She is **steady** with change: she uses AI now and then and learns new tools when she can see the point.
She is a **centrist** with no one to blame, and her biggest concern is the market shrinking.
She splits her job into screen work, which goes first, and **quality checks**, which she hopes to keep.
Her mood tracks time: **alarmed** at two years, anxious at five, uneasy at ten.
biggestWorry: The **2031** picture, close enough to bite but too far to ignore, with thin savings.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training** for late starters, a fair pension, and an honest plan from the firm.
